exemptions.test_tag_refuses_when_a_key_is_unaddress: OVER-DETERMINED, and this is measured rather than argued. Two independent mechanisms produce this exit code for an unaddressable key: the plan-phase refusal, and the tool's own re-lint of its result. Probe 9l removed the first outright (`if reasons:` -> `if not reasons:`) and the run went GREEN — rc was still 2, because the re-lint refused the battery whose key resolves to nothing. A single-subject mutation therefore cannot redden this assertion, and 9l was deleted rather than re-aimed at a claim it did not witness. What the assertion still buys is real and is witnessed next door: 9b keeps the exit code at 2 and reddens the SHA assertion, proving the plan-phase refusal is what stops the WRITE — which is the property 'refuse before writing' actually names.
exemptions.test_tag_appends_to_anchor_lines_rewrite: Reached only when three tags exist and the third is the multi-line claim's closing line. Every mutation that moves a tag off its anchor makes the enumeration refuse, so the tool restores and the rc assertion (9a) reddens first. 9a is this claim's witness one assertion earlier.

The byte-identity half of (i). A mutation that touches a non-anchor line is the same edit as 9k's trailing-newline mutation, which reddens the line-count assertion immediately above it; there is no single-subject mutation that corrupts an interior line while leaving the count intact.

A POSITIVE CONTROL for the assertion above, not an independent claim: it proves the byte-identity check is not vacuous by showing the anchor lines did change. Making it redden requires leaving an anchor untagged, which reddens the count assertion (9d's claim) first.

(ii), the unaddressed-claim claim. AC-9 predicted 9d would redden it while (i) stayed green; measured, any mutation that tags an extra claim also changes (i)'s count of tagged lines, which is asserted first. Recorded as an AC-9 correction rather than reordered, because the count is the stronger assertion of the two.

(iii). AC-9 exempts this explicitly and states the reason: the tool re-lints its own result and restores on any finding, so a battery left addressing dead text keys never reaches this assertion — the rc assertion reddens first.
The exemption half of (iii), same reason as the line above: AC-9's stated re-lint-then-restore exemption.
exemptions.test_tag_adopts_an_existing_tag_instead_: Adoption's byte-identity claim. Any mutation that writes to an adopted line produces a doubled marker, which the enumeration refuses, so the rc assertion (9c) reddens first.
The no-second-marker claim, same path as the line above and unreachable for the same reason — a doubled marker is a refusal, not a surviving second tag.
exemptions.test_tag_appends_after_an_existing_trail: 9f's GREEN control: the run must still succeed for the ordering assertion to mean anything about order rather than about failure. A probe reddening it would be witnessing 'the tool broke', which 9a and 9c already witness.
The resolution half of the trailing-comment case, and AC-9 names it as the control that stays green under 9f. It is reached only when the ordering assertion above it passes.
exemptions.test_tag_refuses_an_append_that_would_ex: A FIXTURE-PREMISE assertion, not a claim about the tool: it pins the fixture's own width so the width arithmetic below cannot drift silently. The s288 precedent exempts fixture premises with this reason (tests/batteries/s288-battery-definition-lint.json).
The fact-of-refusing half. 9n isolates the printed VALUE from it deliberately, and a mutation reddening this one instead is 9g's claim — the tool not refusing at all.
The writes-nothing half of the width refusal. The only mutation that writes here is 9g's skipped width check, which reddens the rc assertion two lines earlier.
The positive control's own consequence: reached only after the control run succeeds, which is 9h's claim.
exemptions.test_dry_run_prints_the_sd_e_measurement: 9i and 9j both keep the dry run exiting 0 on purpose, so this is their shared GREEN control rather than a claim either can witness.
